bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that
bivy.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.

bivy.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
bivy.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other
bivy.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
bivy.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
bivy.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.
bivy.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
bivy.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin
bivy.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other
bivy.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
bivy.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. BURNT BOOT PEAK is climbed from here by fording the Middle Fork — cold and thigh-deep at ordinary summer flows, and not to be attempted in high water — and then working up the northwest side to the gully system and the northeast gully at around 5,800 ft. The boot path to Hardscrabble Lakes leaves the old road about half a mile below the camp, marked by a large broken log lying across the road; it is easy to walk past. Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most
bivy.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.
bivy.notes: The high camp for BIG SNOW MOUNTAIN's east ridge, which is the easier and much less confusing of that peak's two routes. From the boot path junction on the old road the trail climbs steeply and roughly to lower Hardscrabble Lake at about 4,060 ft, and the upper lake is another half mile and 500 ft above it. The path is a climbers' track, not a maintained trail, and the section between the lakes is slabby, brushy and locally class 3 or 4 — this is the hardest walking on the route. From the upper lake the east ridge route goes over a pass at roughly 5,760 ft and then along to the summit at 6,680 ft, with a final few hundred feet that often want microspikes well into summer. The alternative north slope route from Dingford Creek is shorter on paper and involves serious route-finding and bushwhacking whose difficulty depends entirely on how much snow is still lying; parties who have done both generally recommend the east ridge unless the north side is still filled in. The same camp is the natural start for the high traverse west toward IRON CAP MOUNTAIN. Season is essentially August and September; earlier and the slabs below the lakes are running with meltwater. Unlike the Cle Elum-side camps in this zone, the Middle Fork approach was outside the 2026 fire closure — which is the one situation in which the western approach to this range is the correct choice.

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more
bivy.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited on the higher benches above 5,000 ft; keep to durable ground and stay off the boggy meadow.
bivy.notes: The upper-valley camp of the Middle Fork, and the base for IRON CAP MOUNTAIN's south route. From the Dingford Creek gate it is about seven miles of closed road to the horse camp and roughly seven more of trail up the valley — the last stretch through avalanche slopes, wildflowers and deep bracken fern depending on the season — to the Williams Lake junction. Williams Lake sits about half a mile off the main trail and is genuinely secluded, with a good view across to Little Big Chief. From these meadows the route to Iron Cap climbs toward La Bohn Gap and then takes the ridge, with a bit of exposure but generally easy scrambling to the true summit. Two things to be honest about. First, this is a fourteen-mile approach before any climbing starts, so Iron Cap from here is a three-day objective for most parties. Second, La Bohn Gap is equally reachable from Necklace Valley on the East Fork Foss River off Highway 2, on the north side of the divide — a completely separate drive and a shorter approach to the gap, and the right choice if Iron Cap alone is the objective. Come this way when Big Snow, Burnt Boot or the western side of Chimney Rock and Overcoat are also on the list. The same trail continues over Dutch Miller Gap to the Waptus valley, so the Middle Fork and Cle Elum halves of this zone are linked on foot even though they are hours apart by road. Beyond Camp Pedro the route toward Overcoat and Chimney Rock climbs steeply and brushily into the rocky corridor between the Chief summits and crosses a pass at about 6,140 ft to reach the Overcoat Glacier — long, committing, and the reason the Pete Lake side is the standard for Chimney Rock.

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
bivy.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.
bivy.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
bivy.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.

Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.

bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most
bivy.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake

bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that

bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.

bivy.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.

Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.

Continuing up-valley on foot the trail runs about six more miles to the old Camp Pedro area and on toward Dutch Miller Gap. Season is May into October at this elevation, but the peaks above hold snow until July.

bivy.name: Upper Hardscrabble Lake
bivy.capacity: Small and rough — a handful of flat spots on benches and slabs near the outlet, two or three tents at most
bivy.water: The lake, plus snowmelt runnels early in the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Below 5,000 ft by a small margin, but treat it as a no-fire camp regardless — the benches are thin-soiled and there is nothing to burn.

bivy.name: Williams Lake and the upper Middle Fork meadows below Dutch Miller Gap
bivy.capacity: Williams Lake holds a small number of quiet sites, a party or two; the heather and huckleberry benches nearer the gap are informal and can absorb a few more
bivy.water: Williams Lake, the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River, and tarns and snowmelt in the meadows toward the gap

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond and Squaw Lake, Cathedral Pass
bivy.capacity: Peggy's Pond has roughly four well-levelled bivouac spots plus one on a slight slope — small, and it fills. Squaw Lake lower down has a couple of good sites and is the overflow.
bivy.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park at Tucquala Meadows. Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
bivy.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Take the Cathedral Pass trail — not the Deception Pass trail, which leaves the same lot — past Squaw Lake at about 4,800 ft and up easy switchbacks to the pass at roughly 5,600 ft, then the spur west to Peggy's Pond directly beneath the rock. That spur has a short exposed scrambly section that is a genuine obstacle for some parties carrying overnight packs. From the pond the standard southwest face route and the northwest couloir are both short summit days, which is the whole appeal — this is the one peak in the zone with a real climb at the end of a modest approach. The northwest couloir holds snow and is an early-season line; the southwest face is the summer scramble. Hyas Lake, at around 3,550 ft on the Deception Pass trail less than two miles from the same lot, is the low-effort alternative camp with plenty of sites, but it adds 2,000 ft to summit day and is better as a family basecamp than a climbers' one. Honest caveat for 2026: the Deception Pass trail and this whole area were inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer, scheduled to run to the end of October — check before driving out.

bivy.name: Pete Lake and the Lemah Meadows camps
bivy.capacity: Numerous established sites around Pete Lake, enough for a dozen or more parties on a summer weekend; the meadow camps beyond are informal and hold two or three tents each
bivy.water: Reliable all season — the lake itself, the Cooper River along the trail, and Lemah Creek and its north fork above the meadows
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead board, filled out and carried. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve including stock. Campfires are legal at these elevations but the lakeshore is heavily used and a stove is the better manners; no fires above 5,000 ft anywhere in this wilderness.
bivy.notes: The workhorse camp of the entire western half of this zone. From the trailhead at the north end of Cooper Lake the trail runs about four gentle miles along the Cooper River to Pete Lake, and roughly two and a half more to the Lemah Meadows area and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Parties bound for Lemah Mountain and Lemah Two leave the trail here and follow a climbers' path up the north side of Lemah Creek past waterfalls to the meadow at about 3,600 ft, where the creek spreads into shallow ponds; camp at the far end, and expect a thicket of slide alder that is best turned in the timber to the north rather than fought through. Parties bound for Chimney Rock also pass through, but leave the PCT further north — see the Chimney Glacier basin entry. Pete Lake itself is low, forested and mosquito-ridden in early summer, and it is a long way from any summit, so it works as a first-night camp or a bail-out rather than a climbing base. Season is roughly July into October; the valley clears early but the basins above hold snow well into July. The Cooper River road is paved then gravel and passenger-car friendly. Honest caveat for 2026: the Pete Lake trail was inside a large wildfire closure on the Cle Elum Ranger District through late summer, with the closure scheduled to run to the end of October and subject to change — confirm the trail is open before driving out.

bivy.name: Chimney Glacier hanging basin — the big boulder bivy
bivy.capacity: Small. Three or so flat spots around one enormous boulder, including two single-person rectangles tucked under its overhung south side; comfortably two to four climbers, tight beyond that
bivy.water: Meltwater creek running through the basin, dependable while the glacier is melting; late in a dry September it can shrink and want a walk uphill
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit from the Pete Lake trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass to park. Group limit twelve. Campfires prohibited — this is well above 5,000 ft in a fragile basin with no wood to spare. Camp on rock or snow, not on the heather.
bivy.notes: THIS IS CHIMNEY ROCK'S REAL BASE, and it is the reason parties take the Cle Elum side rather than the Middle Fork. From Pete Lake continue to the PCT, turn north, and at the second switchback where the trail starts up toward Waptus Pass leave it westward through open forest, dropping slightly to the North Fork of Lemah Creek at around 3,380 ft. Cross on a log — the crossing is the crux of the approach in high water — and find the boot path on the far side, marked by a large cairn with faded flagging for the first couple of hundred feet. It climbs steeply, roughly 1,400 ft, into the hanging basin below the Chimney Glacier. Aim for the huge boulder near the creek in the middle of the basin. Round trip from the car is on the order of thirty miles for the peak, so this is a two- or three-night trip for most parties, and it puts the East Face and East Face Direct within a reasonable summit day. The same basin serves the standard West Face and South Summit line by way of the glacier and the notch. Best from mid-July to mid-September: earlier and the glacier crossing is straightforward but the approach is a snow slog, later and the ice is bare and crevassed. Expect no company. The alternative from the Middle Fork is described under the Dutch Miller Gap entry and is longer, rougher and more committing for the same summit — the Pete Lake side is the right answer unless the Cle Elum roads are closed.

bivy.name: Escondido Ridge tarns
bivy.capacity: A broad open bench with several flat tent sites and small tarns scattered nearby; four or five parties could spread out without crowding each other
bivy.water: Small tarns and seasonal snowmelt only. They are shallow, they warm up and they can dry out by late September — treat everything and carry a reserve late in the year.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Pete Lake trailhead. Group limit twelve. Above 5,000 ft, so campfires are prohibited outright; the bench is exposed and there is nothing to burn anyway.
bivy.notes: The high camp on the Pacific Crest Trail between Lemah Meadows and Waptus Pass, reached by the long string of switchbacks up onto Escondido Ridge. It is the camp for Little Big Chief Mountain from the south and west, and for the string of Chief summits along that crest. Escondido Lake itself sits below the trail and is invisible from it — the name means hidden and it is earned — so most parties camp on the ridge bench rather than dropping to the lake. The bench is flat, broad and open, with the whole Snoqualmie crest laid out across the valley: Summit Chief, Chimney Rock, Overcoat, Lemah, Bears Breast and Mount Daniel. That view is the reason to be here, and it is also a warning — this is an exposed ridge camp with no shelter in a thunderstorm and no water you can count on. From here Little Big Chief is a long traversing day rather than a short one; parties who want a shorter summit day come at it from Chief Creek on the Waptus side instead. Snow lingers on the switchbacks into July. Honest caveat for 2026: this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail and its eastern access trails were inside the summer fire closure — verify before committing.

bivy.name: Waptus Lake, with Spade Lake above it
bivy.capacity: Large — Waptus has upwards of two dozen established sites strung along the shore and near the outlet, first come first served. Spade Lake above is the opposite: scattered bluff sites for a party or two.
bivy.water: Waptus Lake, the Waptus River and Chief Creek at the lower camps; the lake and small inlet streams at Spade
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Salmon la Sac trailhead. Group limit twelve including stock — this is horse country and the trail is shared. Campfires are permitted at Waptus but banned at Spade and everywhere else above 5,000 ft. Camp at least a hundred feet back from water and off the meadows.
bivy.notes: Waptus is roughly nine miles of easy river trail from Salmon la Sac with only about 800 ft of gain, which makes it the least strenuous long approach in the zone and a genuinely pleasant first night. For climbers here it is the eastern gateway to LITTLE BIG CHIEF MOUNTAIN, which sits immediately southwest of Dutch Miller Gap. The useful camps for that peak are not at the lake but a couple of miles further up the valley, near the bridge over the Waptus River above the lake and near the ford of Chief Creek — call it twelve miles in — and from there the climb is a straight 4,000 ft of off-trail work to the northeast face scramble. Spade Lake is the other well-known destination above Waptus and it is worth being clear about what it is and is not: the spur trail gains nearly 3,000 ft in about three miles of steep, downed-timber forest with scrambly and overgrown sections, and it lands in a rocky cirque on the flank of Mount Daniel. It is a superb, lonely camp and it is NOT a base for Chimney Rock, which lies across the valley on the other side of the crest. Snow lingers in the Spade cirque into July. Honest caveat for 2026: the Waptus and Spade trails were both inside the Cle Elum Ranger District fire closure through the summer — check the status of the closure order before driving to Salmon la Sac.

bivy.name: Park Lakes Basin
bivy.capacity: Several established sites among the trees, meadows and rolling knolls of the basin; three or four parties fit without being on top of each other
bivy.water: The lakes and their connecting streams, plus Glacier Lake just above — reliable through the season
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit. Northwest Forest Pass at the Mineral Creek trailhead. Group limit twelve. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED IN PARK LAKES BASIN specifically, in addition to the general ban above 5,000 ft. Stay off the meadow edges.
bivy.notes: The base for THREE QUEENS, and the reason that peak sits in this zone at all — it shares the Cooper River road with Pete Lake and nothing else. Drive the Cooper River road past Cooper Lake and over Cooper Pass to the Mineral Creek trailhead at around 2,375 ft, then follow the Mineral Creek trail roughly four and a half miles and 2,300 ft up to the basin. The trail crosses Mineral Creek several times on logs and rocks, and in high water those crossings are the hardest part of the day — early season parties should expect at least one that is genuinely unpleasant. From the basin the standard scramble goes up loose slabs, talus and heather to the ridge, and the middle peak's south face and south chimney and the west peak's west ridge are reached from the same camp with a traverse. The rock is loose and the notch below the summit block is exposed with no obvious easy line, so this is a scramble that repays a rope more often than its grade suggests. Many parties skip the camp entirely and do Three Queens as a long day from the car, which is honest and reasonable in good conditions — the basin is worth a night mainly if you want two of the three summits. Best late July through September. Honest caveat for 2026: the Mineral Creek trail was closed by the summer wildfire that took its name from this very peak, along with the Spectacle Lake access and a long stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail; the closure ran into autumn and must be confirmed before any trip.

bivy.name: Hardscrabble Horse Camp, Middle Fork Snoqualmie
bivy.capacity: Large — an old horse camp with a broad clearing and riverside sites near Hardscrabble Creek; several parties, stock included
bivy.water: The Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and Hardscrabble Creek, both right at camp and both reliable
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Dingford Creek gate. Northwest Forest Pass to park at the gate. Group limit twelve including stock. Fires are legal at this elevation and the camp has established rings, but wood is picked over and summer burn bans are common on this district.
bivy.notes: The staging camp for the whole Middle Fork half of this zone, and the answer to the question of what to do with a seven-mile road walk. Forest Road 56 is rough — potholes, ruts and washed river-rock sections that want high clearance — and it is GATED AT DINGFORD CREEK, so the last roughly seven miles to the horse camp are closed road with about 1,300 ft of gain. That stretch is legal and pleasant to bike and most parties do, then walk from here; a mountain bike is the right tool, a gravel bike is survivable. The camp itself is low, forested and buggy, but it is quiet and it sits at the foot of everything. bivy.water: Peggy's Pond itself and the snowmelt feeding it; Squaw Lake below. Both reliable through the normal season.

Peggy's Pond carries a reduced group limit — plan on eight rather than twelve, and midweek is the realistic window for a group of that size. Campfires prohibited: the pond is above 5,000 ft and the basin is heavily used and fragile. Camp on the established pads only.
bivy.notes: The base for CATHEDRAL ROCK, which sits at the far eastern end of this zone and shares nothing but a wilderness boundary with the Middle Fork peaks. Drive the Cle Elum River road north from Salmon la Sac about twelve miles to the Deception Pass and Tucquala Meadows trailhead at the road end; the road is rough gravel with a creek crossing and wants a bit of clearance, and parking is limited enough that you may walk in from further down. bivy.name: Crag View, Squak Glacier
bivy.capacity: The established climbers' camp on the Squak, with room for several parties on gravel benches and snow platforms at the toe of the glacier; quieter than the Easton side even on a summer weekend
bivy.water: No potable water at the trailhead or anywhere on the route. Melt channels run near the moraine edge in early summer and are gone or unreliable by August, so plan on melting snow and carry the fuel for it.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight backcountry permit, but camping below 6,000 ft on this route is prohibited, which is the practical reason Crag View exists where it does. A recreation pass is required to park at the Park Butte trailhead. Party size is capped at 12 once you enter the wilderness, campfires are prohibited, and there is no toilet anywhere on the route — carry blue bags, which are handed out free at the ranger offices in Sedro-Woolley and at Glacier. Nothing may be buried in snow or dropped into a crevasse or moat.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Sherman Peak's Squak Glacier route and it is the site the Mount Baker file does not cover, since everything written there is on the Easton or the Coleman. It sits about 3.5 miles and 3,300 ft above Schriebers Meadow: the Park Butte trail past Sulphur Creek and the meadows, then a climbers' path leaving the trail around 4,600 ft and running up onto the moraine. From here the route makes a rising traverse of the Squak toward Sherman's south ridge, roughly 3,600 ft to the summit. The Squak is an early-season objective and the reason is specific — a bergschrund opens across the line as the season goes on and can shut the route down entirely by late summer, so a July plan is a different proposition from a May one. The lower part of the approach is outside the wilderness and carries snowmobile traffic into early July. Forest Road 13 off Road 12 is gravel and holds snow late; check it before a long drive.

bivy.name: Upper Squak benches, Sulphur moraine and the rock prow
bivy.capacity: Dug snow platforms and moraine gravel for one or two parties along the right-hand edge of the glacier, with a second bench under a rock prow several hundred feet higher; no established sites and no shelter
bivy.water: None. Melt snow. Anything running here in early summer is a bonus and will not be there later in the year.
bivy.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness rules as at Crag View — no permit to camp, recreation pass at the Park Butte trailhead, 12-person party limit, no campfires, all waste packed out in blue bags.
bivy.notes: Parties who want Sherman's summit day short move above Crag View and camp on the Sulphur moraine at the glacier's edge around 7,000 ft, or push on to the flatter ground below the rock prow closer to 7,600 ft. The gain is real, since it takes a good chunk out of the traverse to the south ridge and puts you at the base of the steep snow with the night's freeze still holding. The cost is a fully exposed camp on a volcano's south flank, where wind is the usual reason parties come back down to Crag View, and you are already on glacier and roped to get here. Camping this high also means committing to melt water, which drives fuel weight up. Where exactly the platforms are usable moves year to year with the crevasse pattern, so arrive with daylight to scout rather than in the dark.

bivy.name: Coleman Glacier bivy under the Black Buttes north faces
bivy.capacity: Dug platforms for a party or two on the flats out from the foot of the faces; no established site and nothing to shelter behind
bivy.water: None to rely on. Melt snow. Surface runoff sometimes appears on the rock of the buttes in a hot spell and should not be planned around.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No climbing permit and no overnight permit; camping is dispersed. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park at Heliotrope Ridge. Party limit 12, no campfires, no toilets on the route, waste packed out in blue bags available free from the ranger offices. Registering a climb is voluntary and worth doing.
bivy.notes: Colfax's three north-side ice lines — the Cosley-Houston, the Polish Route and Kimchi Suicide Volcano — all start off the Coleman somewhere near 8,000 ft, and this is the staging ground for a party that does not want to cover the whole approach from the Hogsback on climb morning. The important thing about it is where you do not put the tent: ice and rock come off the Colfax seracs onto this part of the glacier with some regularity, so the usable camping is out on the flats well clear of the fall line, never tucked in against the toe of the face because it looks sheltered. Many parties skip this camp entirely and climb these routes in a long day from the trailhead or from the Hogsback, which is a reasonable answer to the same hazard. These are cold-season routes, roughly late October into May, and the ice changes character completely across that window. Access is the current constraint rather than the camp: Glacier Creek Road washed out in the December 2025 floods and has been closed to vehicles well below the trailhead, open to walkers and bikes at the contractors' discretion with repairs anticipated through 2026 — confirm the road before planning to carry a heavy load.

bivy.name: Cougar Divide meadow camps
bivy.capacity: A handful of small sites in the meadows near the head of the divide; pick rocky ground rather than heather, which recovers slowly here
bivy.water: Better than anywhere else on this side. A creek fed by a lingering snowfield runs at the upper camp through most of the season, and there are ponds along the divide that are worth treating and not drinking untreated. Water gets scarce once the snowfield goes.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit and no climbing permit. The access road is gated seasonally, closed from the start of November until the second week of July for wildlife, which is the single biggest planning constraint on this side of the mountain. Party size 12, no campfires, pack out all waste.
bivy.notes: This is the north-side approach to Hadley Peak and it has nothing to do with the Black Buttes or the Coleman — a party here is on the far side of the mountain from the Heliotrope Ridge climbers. Cougar Divide is an unofficial, unmaintained path along the ridge crest, reached from Wells Creek Road, whose first several miles are badly potholed to the Nooksack bridge and then improve. From the meadows at the head of the divide the ground opens onto Chowder Ridge, and the connection east along the ridge leads to Hadley. The gate opening in July combined with mosquitoes that are genuinely bad here until midsummer pushes the sensible window to mid-August through early October, which is also when the talus is clear and the route is straightforward walking with the odd second-class step.

bivy.name: Skyline Divide crest camps

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road

bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.

bivy.name: Ruth Arm ridge camps below the Ruth Glacier
bivy.capacity: Several flat spots strung along the open ridge, most taking one or two tents; enough for a couple of parties without crowding, more than that and it gets awkward
bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. bivy.water: Snowmelt and a small pond on the traverse from the pass early in the season, then progressively less as summer goes on. By late August plan on carrying up from the pass or melting snow at the glacier toe.
bivy.permit: THIS IS THE IMPORTANT ONE. Everything from Hannegan Pass south along the ridge to the base of the Ruth Glacier is Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so no national park backcountry permit is required here — only the parking pass at the trailhead. The park boundary lies above and beyond, so a party that camps on this ridge and climbs Ruth as a day trip avoids the park permit system entirely. Standard wilderness rules apply: small groups, no fires at this elevation in practice, pack out everything.
bivy.notes: The workhorse high camp for Ruth Mountain and the launching point for the traverse on to Icy Peak, reached by leaving the trail at the pass and following a boot path east then south past a pond, working around cliff bands and along the crest until the ridge runs out at the toe of the Ruth Glacier. Getting here is usually five to six hours from the road with overnight loads. The value of these sites is administrative as much as scenic: they sit on the forest side of the line, so a party turned away from a park reservation can still make this a comfortable two-day climb. Sites are open, exposed and windy, with nothing to shelter behind, and the ridge holds snow well into July in most years. Ruth's summit itself is the last thousand feet of easy glacier above.

bivy.name: Ruth Mountain summit camp
bivy.capacity: A broad snow summit with room to level a few platforms; it is not unusual to share it with another party, but there are no built sites
bivy.water: None. Melt snow, which is normally abundant, or carry from the ridge below. Do not count on running water anywhere near the top.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit required — the summit is inside the park even though the ridge camp below it is not. This falls in a designated cross-country zone rather than a numbered camp, so ask for the zone by name; a valley camp reservation does not cover it. Permits come through the park's online reservation system, with an early-access lottery in March and a general on-sale in late April, and a substantial share held back for walk-ups issued within 24 hours in person. Per-person nightly and transaction fees apply. The Glacier public service centre on the highway west of the trailhead is the nearest place to collect one, and a permit not picked up by late morning on the first day is released. Cross-country zone rules mean camping only on snow, rock or bare ground, never in meadows and never within a hundred feet of water. Food needs an approved canister or a proper hang; the food lockers in this zone are at designated valley camps, not up here.
bivy.notes: Camping on the summit of Ruth is a genuinely popular thing to do rather than an oddity, because the top is a broad snow dome with an extraordinary outlook over Shuksan, Baker, the Pickets and the whole Chilliwack, and because it puts a party well down the traverse toward Icy Peak before the first morning. It is entirely exposed, with no shelter of any kind and nothing to anchor to but snow, so it needs a settled forecast and the discipline to walk back down to the ridge if the weather turns. The cornice line along the summit ridge is real and changes through the season, so pitch back from the edge and look at where the ground drops away before dark rather than after. Snow cover is what makes the site work; late in a thin year the top is rock and heather and much less pleasant.

bivy.name: Notch bivy on the Ruth-Icy ridge
bivy.capacity: Snow platforms for one small party in the first notch below Ruth's summit, with a rougher alternative on a bench above the gullies further along; no established sites
bivy.water: Melt snow. Occasional running water appears at the edges of the small glaciers on a hot afternoon, but nothing that should be planned around.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, in the cross-country zone covering the Ruth and Icy traverse, which the park treats as a higher-occupancy zone. Reserve online or take a walk-up within 24 hours and collect the paperwork in person before the trip; per-person and transaction fees apply. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground only, keep clear of meadows and water, and store food in an approved canister — there is no hardware anywhere along this ridge.
bivy.notes: The natural camp for a party doing the full traverse from Ruth on to Icy Peak, sitting on snow just beyond the first notch northwest of Ruth's summit. It shortens the second day considerably, because from here the route drops the west ridge to a saddle, crosses a flat bench, descends a steep ramp beside the south ridge gully and reaches the low point of the connecting ridge near 5,700 ft before climbing the glacier on Icy's flank. Icy Peak is much the more serious of the two summits, with loose exposed rock and a narrow final ridge, so arriving there rested matters. The bivy is small, on snow, and fully committed — retreat from it means reversing the traverse over Ruth. Conditions on this ridge change quickly through the summer and the connecting terrain is more broken later in the season, which is why most parties go in June or July.

bivy.name: Shoulder camp above Price Lake, between the Price and East Nooksack glaciers
bivy.capacity: Flat rock slabs with room for two or three bivy sacks, snow-covered into midsummer; a small party only, and no facilities
bivy.water: Snowmelt cascades down the cliffs around 5,000 ft on the way up, which is the last dependable water and the place to fill. At camp it is melt or nothing.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone at the head of the Nooksack. Reserved online or issued as a walk-up within 24 hours, collected in person, with per-person and transaction fees. Cross-country rules apply: durable surfaces only, no camping in meadows or within a hundred feet of water, food in an approved canister, and no fires. The lower part of the walk in crosses Mount Baker Wilderness on the forest side, so the parking pass at the road end and the park permit are two separate things you need at once.
bivy.notes: This is the camp for Nooksack Tower and the only established position on the mountain, used by both the classic line on the north side and the much harder south face. It sits on the shoulder dividing the Price Glacier from the Nooksack Cirque, reached by leaving Price Lake, following the boot path onto the moraine as it rounds the north side of the lake and lower glacier, then peeling up left through a small defile onto the ridge where a goat path runs nearly to the slabs. Do not confuse it with the bivy on Shuksan's north face rib, which is a different place approached from the opposite side of the range entirely. From here the north side route drops to the bergschrund and the south face is reached by downclimbing and a rappel to a pocket glacier and a couloir onto the East Nooksack. Nooksack Tower is one of the harder summits in the range, with loose rock throughout and a descent of ten or more rappels, so the camp is a working platform rather than a comfort. Everything about it depends on the approach below being passable, which is the real problem.

bivy.name: Nooksack Cirque river bottom, below the tower
bivy.capacity: Nothing established. Parties make do on gravel bars when the river is low, or on flat ground in the old growth near the point where the route meets the North Fork. One party at a time in practice, and the ground moves year to year.
bivy.water: The river and its tributaries are everywhere and never fail, but the North Fork is heavily glacier-fed and runs opaque with rock flour. Filter from a clear side stream rather than the main channel where you can.
bivy.permit: Split. The lower miles are Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest and then Mount Baker Wilderness, needing only the parking pass and a self-issue wilderness registration. Past the boundary further up the valley it is North Cascades National Park, and a night on that side needs a park backcountry permit for the cross-country zone, arranged in advance or as a walk-up and collected in person before you start. There is no ranger presence out here to sort it out for you, so know which side of the line you intend to sleep on before you leave the road. No fires.
bivy.notes: SAY THIS PLAINLY: there is no real camping in the Nooksack Cirque, and any party heading for Nooksack Tower should expect to improvise a night on gravel or in the trees rather than arrive at a site. The way in is a genuine bushwhack. The spur road dead-ends at Ruth Creek with no bridge, so the trip begins by wading or crossing on whatever log is currently down, and a log that is crossable at dawn can be underwater by afternoon once the day's melt arrives. In early summer Ruth Creek alone can be too high to cross at all, and the North Fork above it is worse. Beyond the creek the route follows two miles of abandoned roadbed, then second growth to the wilderness boundary, then old growth to the river, after which progress depends entirely on whether the gravel bars are exposed or whether you are fighting through riverside brush. Cool weather and low water are what make it work, which is why this valley is best in the autumn — the exact opposite of the season that suits the climbing above. The first ascent party camped near this height on the river before starting up, and little about the ground has become easier since. Treat the water crossings as the crux of the trip, not the climb.

bivy.name: Hannegan trailhead, end of the Ruth Creek road
bivy.capacity: A small set of rough roadside sites at the road end plus informal pullouts along the last miles; a handful of parties, and the parking area fills on summer weekends
bivy.water: Ruth Creek runs below the road and is easy to reach, and side streams cross the lower trail. Reliable all season, but it is glacial and forest runoff — filter rather than just treating.
bivy.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest. A Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park; a Washington state Discover Pass does NOT work at a Forest Service fee site. No overnight backcountry permit is needed to sleep here or anywhere between the road and the pass, though a free self-issue wilderness registration at the trailhead is the norm once you walk in. Fires are subject to seasonal restrictions and are worth checking against the current burn ban rather than assumed.
bivy.notes: This is where nearly every trip in the zone starts, and it is the answer for a party that drives out after work and wants a short night before an alpine start on Ruth. It is also the base for Mount Sefrit, which is normally done car-to-car from a pullout a few miles back down the road and has no camp of its own worth listing. Road access has been the weak link: a washout near the end of FS 32 cut vehicle access to the sites at the road end for a period, a bypass has since been built above the damaged section, and both the road and the trailhead have a history of being reachable in one season and not the next. Confirm the road is open to the end before committing to the drive out. In winter and spring the road beyond the Goat Mountain trailhead runs under avalanche terrain and the last miles are usually snowbound well into spring.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground

bivy.name: Beckler River Campground

bivy.name: Beckler River Campground
bivy.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.
bivy.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
bivy.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. bivy.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.
bivy.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system when open. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee.
bivy.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong. bivy.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin

bivy.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. bivy.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. bivy.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.

bivy.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses

bivy.name: Beckler River Campground

bivy.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
bivy.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. Sort that out before you commit.
bivy.notes: These are the only walls in this zone big enough that a party sleeps on them. The Jotunheim cirque holds the North and South Norwegian Buttresses, separated by a deep cleft, and the long free lines up the north buttress run to well over a dozen pitches of sustained climbing. Ledges are scarce and small — the established practice on the modern free routes is to bring a portaledge rather than count on finding a stance, with one known used bivouac high on the north buttress above the twelfth pitch. Treat that as the shape of the problem: this is a hanging bivouac by default, not a ledge camp. Anything you want, including water, comes up with you from the lake. Weather is the other half of it: the wall faces the Skykomish valley and takes the full brunt of a westerly, and the approach gully and the slabs below turn into moving water in rain, so the retreat is worse than the climb. Best conditions are a settled dry spell in high summer, with the caveat that this is low country and can be hot and buggy at the same time.

bivy.name: Middle Peak crest bivouac, Mount Index traverse
bivy.capacity: One small party. A flat patch on the ridge crest between the two Middle Peak summits — a stance, not a site.
bivy.water: Snow on the crest into early summer, and nothing at all once it goes. On a dry traverse you carry water for the whole ridge or you drop off it.
bivy.permit: No permit for a bivouac on the ridge. The trailhead day-use rules below still apply to the car. Fires are out of the question up here regardless of the current ban.
bivy.notes: The traverse of Mount Index's three peaks is the one objective in this zone that is genuinely an overnight rather than a long day, and this is where parties sleep. The line links South, Middle and North Peaks along a crest of loose ridges and gullies with rappels between them, and the recorded practice is a flat spot right on the crest between the two Middle Peak summits with snow nearby, which solves the water problem in early season. Parties who have done it in a push describe going light and treating the bivouac as an emergency plan that they were glad to have and glad not to need — take minimal gear rather than a full camp, because everything you carry has to come over some genuinely poor rock. Approach is the Lake Serene trail as for everything else on the mountain. The rock on Index is famously rotten and the descent options off the ridge are limited, so committing to a bivouac here means committing to finishing the traverse; do not plan it as a place to sit out bad weather.

bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. It sits almost directly under Grotto Mountain and is a sensible base for the Beckler-side objectives, for Baring and the Barclay Creek peaks about fifteen minutes back down the highway, and for anyone wanting a shower-free but civilised night before an early start. Being this low it is usable well outside the alpine season — a real advantage in a zone where several of the objectives are winter routes and everything above 3,000 ft is snowbound. Do not treat it as an approach camp; it is a place to sleep in the valley with a proper toilet and a fire ring, twenty to forty minutes' drive from any of the trailheads.

bivy.name: Beckler River Campground
bivy.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.
bivy.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
bivy.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. If the campground is full or closed for the season, the upper Beckler road corridor and its spurs are national forest land where dispersed camping is allowed with no permit — the standing rules are to camp at least 100 ft from water, use an existing pullout rather than making a new clearing, stay a maximum of fourteen days in one spot, and obey whatever fire restriction is current. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.

bivy.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.
bivy.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system when open. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee.
bivy.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong. It sits about eleven miles up the Index-Galena Road from US 2 at roughly 1,200 ft on the North Fork Skykomish, which put it within twenty minutes of the Lake Serene trailhead and made it the obvious base for Mount Index. Flooding washed out the Index-Galena Road near mileposts 10 and 14, the road is gated closed through that section with permanent repairs estimated in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the county has said environmental review and permitting may take several years. The campground is inaccessible and closed as a result, and the neighbouring campground further up the same road is closed with it. Confirm the road status before counting on it; if the gate is still shut, the working substitutes for an Index-area night are Money Creek down the highway or a dispersed pullout on the Beckler system. Nothing on the Reiter Road side fills the gap — the lower Reiter Foothills road corridor is state land signed day use only with no camping and a Discover Pass required, which is the approach used for Mount Persis, so plan Persis as a day out from the valley.

bivy.name: Barclay Lake
bivy.capacity: Several established lakeside sites strung along the north shore, plus a few set back in the trees. Popular, and full most summer weekends — it is one of the easiest overnight walks on this stretch of highway. Two vault toilets serve the lake.
bivy.water: The lake and Barclay Creek run all year. Treat everything; this is a heavily used shoreline. In hard winter the lake freezes and the creek runs under snow.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit. The trail corridor and the lake itself were deliberately left OUT of the Wild Sky Wilderness so that larger groups could keep using them, so the twelve-person wilderness party limit does not apply at the lake — but it does apply the moment you leave the corridor onto any of these peaks. Parking at the trailhead takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is not valid. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire, and camp only in the existing sites.
bivy.notes: This is the one genuinely established camp in the zone and the obvious base for the Barclay Creek peaks. It sits at 2,420 ft in a narrow trench with Baring Mountain's north face rising straight out of the south shore and Merchant Peak and Gunn Peak on the north side, so nearly every objective on that road starts from here or from the road below it. Two miles and about 200 ft of net gain from the trailhead, which makes it a realistic place to sleep the night before rather than a committing carry. From the east end of the lake, boot paths climb north to Stone and Eagle Lakes and give the standard way onto Merchant and Gunnshy. Note that Baring's north face and Dolomite Tower are reached by leaving the trail and grinding up the south side of the valley — brushy, loose, and a different proposition from the walk to the lake. Realistically most parties here climb car-to-car and use this camp only if they want a pre-dawn start without the two-hour drive, or if they got benighted and walked out late. One current caveat: the footlog over Barclay Creek on the approach has been removed for safety and a replacement has no date, so plan on a ford or a log-hop and expect that to be genuinely awkward during spring runoff.

bivy.name: Eagle Lake and the old cabin
bivy.capacity: A handful of informal sites around the shore, plus an old timber cabin on the lakeshore that sleeps a few and is first-come, first-served. Do not count on the cabin being free, and do not plan around it.
bivy.water: The lake, plus small creeks crossing the trail on the last stretch. Reliable through summer and autumn.
bivy.permit: Inside the Wild Sky Wilderness, so the twelve-person party limit applies and stock and mechanised travel are out. No fee permit system, but leave-no-trace practice matters here — the shoreline is small and gets hammered. Check the current campfire ban; stoves are the sensible default. The cabin is a leftover from private use in the early twentieth century, maintained informally by whoever passes through: if you use anything left inside, replace it.
bivy.notes: The high camp for the north side of the Barclay Creek trench, at about 3,900 ft. Two ways in, and they are very different. From the east end of Barclay Lake a steep, rough, unmaintained two miles climbs directly to it — that is the line a climber coming off Merchant or Gunnshy would use. The other is a back door from the Beckler River road system: drive FR 65 to FR 6510 to FR 6514, park at an unmarked hairpin, and walk about four miles with only 500 ft of gain, which is far and away the gentlest approach to any high water in this zone. That second option matters because it is the same road that gets you near Eagle Rock and Grotto Mountain, so one drive can serve a camp and an objective. Snow lingers in the basin into June most years. It is a genuinely pleasant place to sleep and a good fallback when Barclay Lake is full.

bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.capacity: No established sites at all. What exists is a scatter of flat spots among the boulders and slabs on the south side of the basin, below the walls. Room for a couple of small parties at most, and none of it is comfortable.
bivy.water: The lake, and meltwater running off the slabs and the gullies above into midsummer. Later in the season the runnels dry and the lake is the only certainty.
bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Camping and campfires are prohibited within a quarter mile of Lake Serene, and the trailhead itself is signed day use only, open sunrise to sunset, with no overnight parking. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. So a legal bivy has to be well beyond the lake, out toward the base of the walls, and even then the car is the problem rather than the ground.
bivy.notes: This is the honest awkward centre of the zone. Everything on Mount Index — the Main Peak's north approach, the Hourglass Gully in winter, the North Peak's Northeast Buttress, and the whole Jotunheim cirque with the Norwegian Buttresses — starts from this trailhead at 600 ft and climbs about 2,000 ft in under four miles to the lake at roughly 2,520 ft, then traverses the shore over talus and car-sized boulders to reach the base of the walls in another fifteen or twenty minutes. That is a short, brutal approach rather than a long one, which is exactly why parties overwhelmingly do these routes car-to-car and why there is no camp here. Where a bivy genuinely happens is at the foot of the buttresses, beyond the quarter-mile ring, on slab and talus. Take a pad and expect rock, not ground. The serious caveat is rockfall: large natural releases have been observed coming off North Index and out of the cleft between the buttresses, so parties are advised to stay low along the lake until they can go straight up to the base — and by the same logic, do not sleep in the fall line of that gully. Winter changes the picture completely: Hourglass Gully is a snow-and-ice objective and the basin is under a deep avalanche-fed snowpack, so a winter bivy here is a snow camp with the walls above you loaded. The day-use hours mean an alpine start is a very early drive from town rather than a walk from a tent.

bivy.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses

bivy.name: Lake Serene basin and the talus under the Norwegian Buttresses

bivy.permit: Read this before planning anything here. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee; a Discover Pass is not valid. bivy.name: On-wall ledges, Jotunheim and the Norwegian Buttresses
bivy.capacity: One or two climbers per stance. There is no ledge system here that a party can spread out on.
bivy.water: None on the wall. Carry everything from the lake, which is the last certain water — top off before starting up the talus.
bivy.permit: National forest land, no permit for a bivouac on the route. The quarter-mile camping ban is measured from the lake, so a stance high on the wall is not the issue; the trailhead's day-use parking rules still are, and a multi-day route means leaving a car overnight at a day-use lot. bivy.name: Money Creek Campground
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, most of them accessible. Reservable, with a couple held first-come first-served. Picnic tables, vault toilets, and a swimming hole on the river.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground. The South Fork Skykomish runs alongside.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee, booked through the federal reservation system or taken first-come at the two unreserved sites. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Fourteen-day stay limit. Check the current forest-wide campfire ban before planning a fire.
bivy.notes: The nearest drive-in campground to the middle of this zone, on the old highway loop south of US 2 at about milepost 46, roughly three miles west of Skykomish and low down at 880 ft in old growth on the river. bivy.name: Beckler River Campground
bivy.capacity: 26 sites, 22 single and four double, all reservable. Picnic tables and vault toilets. No stock or pack animals.
bivy.water: Potable water from a solar pump at the campground, and the Beckler River itself.
bivy.permit: Standard national forest campground fee through the federal reservation system. Day use needs a Northwest Forest Pass, Interagency pass or the day fee. Open roughly May through September, so it is not a winter option. Fourteen-day stay limit, no fireworks, and a food storage order applies — check the current campfire ban.
bivy.notes: A mile and a half up the Beckler River road (FR 65) from US 2 just west of milepost 50, at about 1,000 ft. This is the natural base for the eastern end of the zone: the same road, continuing north and then west onto FR 6510 and FR 6514, is what gets you to Eagle Rock, to the road end at roughly 3,500 ft used for Grotto Mountain, and to the gentle back-door approach to Eagle Lake. Those spurs are rough, gated in places, and can be locked without warning, so check the gate on your way in rather than discovering it on your way out. Being a valley campground it says nothing about conditions up high; expect snow on the FR 6514 spurs well into spring.

bivy.name: Troublesome Creek Campground
bivy.capacity: 25 sites, 24 single and one double, normally reservable. Picnic tables, vault toilets, a footbridge over the creek, and river access.
bivy.water: Potable water from a solar pump when the site is open, plus the creek and the North Fork Skykomish.

bivy.notes: Listed here because it is the classic answer to where to sleep near Index, and because that answer is currently wrong.
